source.title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems

accepted.question_text: What mathematical principle explains the origin and distinctiveness of topological atoms in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules (QTAIM)? A topological atom is an atomic basin in real three-dimensional space obtained from the gradient vector field of the one-electron density: nuclei are (3,-3) attractors, gradient paths terminating at an attractor form its basin, and interatomic surfaces are zero-flux boundaries. Since other three-dimensional quantum divided basins can satisfy the net zero-flux equation without being these atomic basins, can QTAIM justify why topological atoms, rather than merely any net-zero-flux basins, are the physically natural quantum subsystems?
accepted.context_brief: Origin and distinctiveness of topological atoms

evidence.quote: 2.1. What is the very origin of the topological atom?

The vector field reveals maxima, termed also (3, -3) critical points [1], at the position of nuclei, which act as the attractors of the gradient field, while all the gradient paths terminating at an attractor disclose the basin of the attractor, i.e. the atomic basin.

The presence of the quantum divided basins reveals that the topological atoms are not uniquely derivable from the net zero-flux equation and they are just a tiny subset of the whole 3D objects satisfying the net zero-flux equation. In other words, the objects compatible to the mathematical fabric of the subsystem quantum mechanics are not exclusively the topological atoms. Thus, the question arises that what makes the topological atoms distinct?

accepted.question_text: Can one prove from the quantum theory of a free atom that the ground-state one-electron density has a single attractor, a (3,-3) critical point, at the nucleus and decays monotonically away from the nucleus, rather than treating this density topology as a computationally observed but unproved conjecture?
accepted.context_brief: Monotonicity and single attractor of free-atom density

evidence.quote: It is well-known computationally that the ground state of a free atom reveals a single attractor, a (3, -3) critical point, at the position of nucleus while the atom decays “monotonically” far from the nucleus [1,54,55] (check Figure 1), however, from theoretical viewpoint, this is not a proven conjecture yet [56-59].
As discussed, this conjecture is closely related to the unproven conjecture of the monotonicity of and probably one needs to prove the monotonicity before proving the present conjecture.

accepted.question_text: How do Coulombic interactions between nuclei and electrons determine the topology of the molecular one-electron density so that topological atoms arise naturally? In particular, what mathematical mechanism makes nuclear attractors the usual attractors of the density-gradient field in Coulombic molecular systems, whereas replacing Coulomb interactions by harmonic interactions can produce a different density topology?
accepted.context_brief: Coulombic origin of molecular density topology

evidence.quote: This reasoning was implicitly confirmed when we tried to apply the QTAIM analysis to a hypothetical model of molecule where the coulombic interactions between electrons and nuclei were replaced by the harmonic potential, i.e. the Hookean model of molecule [28].

The results of the analysis on the Hookean H2+ demonstrated that instead of two attractors in on each of the nuclei, a single attractor emerges in the middle of the nuclei [28]. Evidently, the fact that the attractors of in the coulombic systems are usually revealed only on the nuclei is not something trivial and is tied intrinsically to the nature of the interaction of nuclei and electrons. Accordingly, the naturalness problem may be cast in a more concrete language: How the coulombic interactions between nuclei and electrons dictate the topology of the one-electron density in a way that the concept of the topological atom arises naturally?

accepted.question_text: For a Coulombic molecular system with N electrons and q clamped nuclei, is there always a critical internuclear distance for each pair of nuclei such that, whenever all internuclear distances are larger than their critical values, the gradient of the molecular one-electron density has exactly q nuclear (3,-3) critical points and no non-nuclear attractors; and can the statement that most molecules have equilibrium internuclear distances larger than these critical distances be made mathematically precise and proved?

evidence.quote: Based on this background, let us now formulate the idea of the naturalness of the topological atoms as a mathematical conjecture:

Evidently, the last part of the conjecture, namely the fact that in “most” molecules the equilibrium inter-nuclear distances are larger than the critical distances, is hard to properly paraphrased mathematically and probably hardest part to be proved.

accepted.question_text: Can the critical-distance explanation of topological-atom naturalness be extended from point-charge Coulomb external potentials to larger classes of external potentials, such as finite-nucleus models or other marginal modifications, by proving that the topology of the one-electron density is independent of those marginal changes?
accepted.context_brief: Extending density-topology conjectures beyond point nuclei

evidence.quote: Also, it is interesting to extend the conjecture to a larger class of external potentials, e.g. those derived from the finite nucleus models [76], since the topology of the one-electron density is probably independent from marginal modifications of the external potential (for a similar proposal see [23]).

accepted.question_text: Can the subsystem virial and energy analysis used in QTAIM be generalized to non-equilibrium molecular geometries where Hellmann-Feynman forces are not zero, so that topological-atom energy concepts apply to nuclear vibrations, chemical reactions, and other non-equilibrium structures?

evidence.quote: The fact that the HF forces are assumed to be null from the outset of the analysis restricts the whole analysis only to the equilibrium geometries. This is somehow annoying since because of nuclear vibrations as well as chemical reactions the QTAIM analysis of non-equilibrium geometries is also desirable.

There have been some attempts to extend the analysis beyond equilibrium geometries when the HF forces are not null and these have been summarized by Keith (see chapter 3 in [3]). But, none of the proposed schemes is satisfying as stressed by the author himself (a possible tentative route to solve this problem have been proposed by present author recently that needs to be worked out in detail [45]).

accepted.question_text: How can one define an origin-independent energy for a topological atom when the molecular Hamiltonian contains non-Coulombic, inhomogeneous, or marginally modified potential-energy terms? The desired definition must work when the usual Coulombic homogeneity used in the subsystem virial theorem fails, including potentials that are sums of homogeneous terms of different degrees or are not finitely decomposable into homogeneous terms.

evidence.quote: 2.2. How to extend the concept of topological atom’s “energy” for non-coulombic interactions?

Any marginal modification of the coulombic potential energy in a molecular system, e.g. using any of the finite nucleus models instead of the point charge model [76] or adding terms corresponding to various small magnetic interactions [77,78], destroys the homogeneity of the potential energy function, making the originally proposed procedure useless.

The local version of the subsystem virial theorem is now: and evidently, this equation cannot be used to propose a proper form for to guarantee the origin independence of the topological atom’s energy.

However, this procedure is too crude to be seen as a proper solution and we leave the proper definition of topological atom’s energy upon marginal modification of the coulombic potential as an open problem.

accepted.question_text: What is the most efficient definition of the state of a topological atom? A satisfactory definition should specify what information constitutes an atomic state and should make the atom’s properties practically deducible from that state, rather than merely listing all atomic properties or invoking a formal existence argument that the atomic one-electron density determines them.
accepted.context_brief: Practical definition of a topological atom state

evidence.quote: 2.3. What is the most efficient way of introducing the concept of the topological atom’s “state”?

The concept of “state” is central in physics and by definition, knowing the state of a system means that all accessible information for the system is at hand, thus, it is legitimate to ask that how the state of a topological atom must be defined.

Taking all these problems while the Bader and Beker’s reasoning must be seen a step forward the question remains whether one may define the state of topological atom in a way that the properties of the atom may be deduced from this definition in practice.

accepted.question_text: Can explicit functionals of a topological atom’s one-electron density, or a successful variational principle based on that density or another atomic function, be constructed so that topological-atom properties can be computed rather than only formally asserted to exist?
accepted.context_brief: Explicit atomic density functionals and variational principles

accepted.question_text: Can the literature and formalism of open quantum systems be used to redefine or improve the efficient state description of a topological atom, treating an atom in a molecule as an open subsystem whose properties must be inferred from an appropriate state specification?

evidence.quote: Taking the large and diverse literature on the open quantum systems, flourished in the last decades [89,90], the time is ripe to reconsider the problem of efficient definition of topological atom’s state in the light of these new developments.

accepted.question_text: Do interatomic zero-flux surfaces act as holograms for topological atoms by encoding the right amount of information needed to deduce basin properties from boundary data, rather than requiring full three-dimensional property densities inside each atomic basin?

evidence.quote: 2.4. Do the interatomic-surfaces act as “hologram” for the topological atoms?
In this context, it is possible to demonstrate that to determine many properties of the topological atoms just knowing what goes on the interatomic-surfaces suffices.

Therefore, the considered example is not something exceptional and the subsystem hypervirial theorem also entails the same type of the relationship between the “bulk” and the “boundary” of a topological atom and one may claim that just knowing the currents at the boundaries is enough to deduce the basin properties.
All these are in line with the idea that the inter-atomic surfaces may be act as holograms, i.e. coding the right amount

accepted.question_text: Can one derive a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms that goes beyond the subsystem hypervirial theorem and covers all conceivable topological-atom properties, including properties such as atomic energy and electron localization or delocalization indices that are not evidently obtained from known property currents on interatomic surfaces?
accepted.context_brief: General Gauss-like theorem for all atomic properties

evidence.quote: While all these seem to be in favor of the idea of the holographic nature of the inter-atomic surfaces, there are properties like the energy of the topological atom, discussed in the previous subsection, which does not seem to be deducible from the known property currents on the inter-atomic surfaces.

One may add to this list the electron localization and the delocalization indices of the topological atoms, which are measures of the electron sharing between two atomic basins [97-99] (see also E7.1 appendix in [1]).

It seems that the idea of the hologram to be generally true, one needs to derive a general Gauss-like theorem for the topological atoms that goes beyond the subsystem hypervirial theorem and covers all conceivable properties of the topological atoms.

accepted.question_text: Can QTAIM be reformulated as a practical boundary-only theory in which calculations use only the two-dimensional interatomic surfaces and still yield the properties of the three-dimensional topological atoms, and what analytical differential geometry of interatomic surfaces is needed to make such a holographic formulation work?

evidence.quote: The next step will be to answer the question whether such holographic property may be used practically namely, one may derive a theory that only works with the inter-atomic surface, i.e. boundaries/2D surfaces, and yield the properties of the topological atoms without any need to refer to 3D space; this directs us toward the more general idea of duality [100-103].

Accordingly, the analytical differential geometry of the inter-atomic surfaces must be also considered more thoroughly [104-108], seeking for general traits of these surfaces that may help to apply the idea of the holography in practice.

accepted.question_text: Does QTAIM, or do topological atoms themselves, have non-trivial dual formulations? Candidate duals include viewing a topological atom’s density in three-dimensional Euclidean space as equivalent to a free-atom density in non-Euclidean space, and viewing property currents of a topological atom as flows on the boundaries of a stationary but non-equilibrium thermodynamic open system.
accepted.context_brief: Non-trivial duals of QTAIM and topological atoms

evidence.quote: Both of these proposals are examples of dualities; a topological atom, or more precisely, in 3D Euclidian space may “equally” be seen as a free atom, or, in a non-Euclidian space [109], and the property currents of a topological atom may “equally” be seen as flows in the boundaries of a stationary but non-equilibrium thermodynamic system [110].
Whether the QTAIM as a theory or the topological atoms as the target objects of this theory may have non-trivial duals as proposed above is an interesting open question that needs further scrutiny.

accepted.question_text: How should a quantum subsystem, or a division into system plus environment, be introduced when the principles of quantum mechanics do not provide a clear recipe, and how should QTAIM’s own subsystem principles and axioms be extended as part of an ongoing research programme rather than treated as a finalized theory?
accepted.context_brief: Principles for quantum subsystem theories and QTAIM extensions

evidence.quote: The idea of subsystem is foreign to quantum mechanics and the principles of the theory do not give a clear recipe how a quantum subsystem, or division to system plus environment, must be introduced.

The fact that these theories do not directly flow from the basic principles of quantum mechanics and contain their own principles and axioms give them their own unique identity, distinct from quantum mechanics; this identity includes their mathematical formalism as well as specific capabilities.

All these examples cast doubt that the final chapter of the QTAIM has been written yet and as proposed recently [27,38,79], the QTAIM must be seen as an ongoing “research programme” rather than a “finalized theory”.

accepted.question_text: Can one develop a liquid model of charge density in atoms-in-molecules theory in which a principal parameter is the viscosity experienced by migrating critical points, and can the currently incomplete mechanics of charge density be extended into new models that answer old problems?
accepted.context_brief: Liquid model and mechanics of charge density

evidence.quote: Could one develop a liquid model of the charge density, a principle parameter being the viscosity experienced by migrating critical points?

While there is a mechanics of the charge density, it is not complete and the theory of atoms in molecules offers opportunities for the formulation of new models in the search for answers to old problems
